https://fever-clinical-guide.vercel.app/.text: Fever Clinical Guide Fever Clinical Guide Assessment, tests, diagnosis and treatment. Built from Harrison’s Ch. 18–20, with 2024–2026 updates. Assess a febrile patient Patient group Adult / older child Child under 5 years Infant under 3 months Temperature (°C) Duration of fever (days) Rash None Non-blanching / purpuric Other rash (see Rash tab) Red flags Hypotension, shock or capillary refill ≥3 s Neck stiffness, altered mental state, seizure Respiratory distress or SpO₂ low Bilious vomiting, rigid abdomen Mottled / ashen skin, weak cry Context Immunocompromised, on anticytokine therapy, steroids or NSAIDs Heat exposure, strenuous exercise, or drug that impairs sweating; skin hot and dry New medication in the past weeks Travel to tropics, tick or animal exposure, or outbreak contact Recurrent episodes with fever-free intervals CRP/ESR raised on repeated tests Get assessment Fever and rash Classify the dominant lesion and distribution first (Harrison Table 19-1), then use the history: immune status, drugs, travel, animals, ticks, vaccines. Rash pattern Fever of unknown origin Definition (all four) Fever ≥38.3 °C (101 °F) on at least two occasions Illness lasting ≥3 weeks No known immunocompromise Still unexplained after thorough history, examination and the obligatory tests below Inflammation of unknown origin (IUO): same, but raised CRP/ESR on several occasions for ≥3 weeks without documented fever. Same workup. Step 1. Obligatory investigations First stop antibiotics and glucocorticoids if safe, and stop or replace drugs to exclude drug fever (fever persisting >72 h after stopping the drug makes it unlikely). Exclude thermometer manipulation. Step 2. Look for potentially diagnostic clues (PDCs) PDCs present: guided tests aimed at the suspected disease only. Screening tests have very low yield without PDCs. PDCs absent or misleading: cryoglobulins and fundoscopy, then FDG-PET/CT (or labelled leukocyte scintigraphy or gallium scan if unavailable), especially when CRP/ESR is raised. Repeat history and examination regularly; the diagnostic clue often appears late. Step 3. After imaging Abnormal scan: confirm with biopsy or culture. Normal scan: repeat history and exam, PDC-driven invasive tests. Still nothing: chest and abdominal CT; temporal artery biopsy if ≥55 years. Stable: follow up for new PDCs, consider NSAID. Deteriorating: further tests or a therapeutic trial. Consider a second opinion at an FUO expert centre. Updated evidence The 2024 EANM consensus on FDG-PET/CT in FUO/IUO reports a diagnostic yield or helpfulness of 50–60%, and places it early in the pathway. It outperforms conventional CT for reaching a final diagnosis. Glucocorticoids rapidly abolish pathological FDG uptake, so avoid them before the scan. A low-carbohydrate diet beforehand reduces physiological myocardial uptake when endocarditis is a concern. Common causes (pooled studies) Region Infection Non-infectious inflammatory Malignancy No diagnosis Western Europe 17% 25% 10% 37% Middle East 66% 15% 7% 8% Asia 42% 20% 13% 18% Medians. Tuberculosis is the leading infection in many non-Western cohorts. In the elderly, giant cell arteritis and polymyalgia rheumatica are most frequent. Lymphoma is the commonest neoplasm. Treatment of FUO Avoid empirical antibiotics, glucocorticoids or antituberculous drugs unless the patient is deteriorating, neutropenic or haemodynamically unstable. Positive TST/IGRA, granulomatous disease, anergy or sarcoidosis unlikely: a trial of antituberculous therapy; reconsider if no response by 6 weeks. Colchicine for suspected familial Mediterranean fever. NSAIDs for adult-onset Still’s disease. Glucocorticoids for giant cell arteritis and polymyalgia rheumatica once lymphoma and infection are reasonably excluded. Anakinra trial for suspected IL-1-mediated disease after later-stage tests. Prognosis of unexplained FUO is favourable; mortality is driven by the underlying disease. Treatment of fever Decide whether to treat Fever is a regulated response, not an illness. Antipyretics do not delay recovery from viral or bacterial infection, and are not contraindicated. In suspected bacterial infection, withholding them can help judge response to an antibiotic. Treat actively when: pre-existing cardiac, pulmonary or CNS impairment (oxygen consumption rises about 13% per °C above 37), a history of febrile or non-febrile seizure in a child (Harrison), or marked symptoms such as headache, myalgia and arthralgia. Agents Paracetamol (acetaminophen): preferred first line. Equal to aspirin in fever reduction without platelet or gastric effects. NSAIDs (ibuprofen): effective; caution with platelets, GI tract, kidneys. Aspirin: avoid in children (Reye’s syndrome). Parenteral or rectal forms if the patient cannot take oral drugs. Glucocorticoids: antipyretic but mask disease; use only for specific diagnoses. Dose by the product label and the patient’s weight, renal and hepatic function. Check local formulary. Indian medicine brand reference Verified product listings checked 2 November 2026. One sourced example per medicine (maximum five); brands are examples, not endorsements. Prices are indicative listed MRP for the stated pack, may vary by batch/location, and are not a treatment cost estimate. Where only the marketer is verified, it is labelled explicitly; check the pack for the manufacturing site. Oral adult tablets do not define a paediatric dose or substitute for rectal/injectable formulations. Prescribing must follow diagnosis, age/weight, organ function and the current product label. Paracetamol: check all combination products to avoid duplicate dosing. Ibuprofen / aspirin: avoid in suspected dengue or bleeding, dehydration or significant renal disease; check other NSAIDs and anticoagulants. Aspirin is not a routine childhood antipyretic. Prednisolone and colchicine: prescription medicines for specific diagnoses, not routine treatment of undifferentiated fever. Colchicine has important renal/hepatic and drug-interaction constraints. Specialist IL-1 medicines: Indian brand verification Anakinra and canakinumab are mentioned in this guide. No routine Indian-market brand was verified in this review; no local price or Indian brand is asserted. Overseas products Kineret and Ilaris appear in specialist sourcing listings; these are not counted as Indian brands. Confirm local regulatory access, supply and cold chain with the specialist hospital pharmacy. Anakinra sourcing reference · Canakinumab sourcing reference Children under 5 (NICE NG143, last updated 2021) Do not use antipyretics only to lower the temperature in an otherwise well child; they do not prevent febrile seizures. Give paracetamol or ibuprofen if the child appears distressed. If distress persists, switch to the other agent. Do not give both together; alternate only if distress recurs before the next dose. Safety-net parents: seek help if the child looks worse, has a fit, develops a non-blanching rash, or fever lasts 5 days. Hyperthermia and hyperpyrexia Hyperthermia (heat stroke): set point unchanged, hot dry skin, does not respond to antipyretics . Cool physically; see Harrison Ch. 465. Hyperpyrexia >41.5 °C: often CNS haemorrhage or severe infection. Cooling blankets only together with oral antipyretics in fever. In CNS bleeding or trauma, lowering core temperature protects the brain. Special settings Anticytokine therapy (anti-TNF, IL-6, IL-17): fever is blunted. Low-grade fever warrants early, rigorous workup for TB, fungal and opportunistic infection. Newborns, elderly, chronic liver or renal failure, steroid users: may have infection without fever. Autoinflammatory disease: IL-1 blockade (anakinra, canakinumab) reduces fever. https://cardinal-manifestations-assistan.text: Cardinal Manifestations Clinical Assistant Cardinal Manifestations Assistant Harrison’s 21st ed. Part 2 · Ch. 21–28 · definitions, pathophysiology, assessment, tests, treatment · guidelines checked Oct 2026 • Syncope • Reflex: vasodepressor (sympathetic withdrawal), cardioinhibitory (vagal bradycardia/asystole) or mixed. Orthostatic: autonomic failure, drugs, volume loss. Cardiac: arrhythmia (brady/tachy, long QT, Brugada, CPVT) or structural disease (AS, HCM, ischaemia, PE). • Chest pain, dyspnoea, abdominal pain or headache before event • Syncope during exertion or supine • Palpitations immediately before syncope • Known structural heart disease / heart failure • Family history of sudden death or channelopathy • ECG: ischaemia, AV block, bifascicular block, QRS ≥120 ms, long QT, Brugada, pre-excitation, AF, NSVT • Detailed history incl. witness account, triggers, prodrome, drugs • Supine and 3-min standing BP/HR (orthostatic hypotension: ≥20 systolic / ≥10 diastolic drop) • Cardiac and neurological examination • 12-lead ECG in all patients • Echocardiogram if structural disease suspected or abnormal exam/ECG • Exercise test if syncope during/after exertion • EP study only when high pretest probability (e.g., prior MI/scar, bifascicular block) • Avoid routine neuroimaging, carotid duplex or EEG • Reflex: reassurance, education, avoid triggers, hydration/salt, isometric counterpressure manoeuvres (abdominal tensing most effective) • Orthostatic hypotension: stop culprit drugs, staged rising, fluids/salt, abdominal binder, then fludrocortisone, midodrine or droxidopa • Cardiac: treat the cause — pacing for AV block/sinus disease, ICD/ablation/drugs for VT, valve surgery, etc. • Dizziness & Vertigo • Acute continuous vertigo with vascular risk factors • Normal head impulse test with acute vertigo (HINTS central pattern) • Skew deviation • New severe headache or neck pain • Diplopia, dysarthria, limb ataxia, numbness, weakness • Unable to walk or sit unaided • Unilateral hearing loss with acute vertigo (consider AICA stroke) • Characterise: timing, triggers, duration, associated symptoms • Eye movements, nystagmus, head impulse test, test of skew (HINTS only in AVS with nystagmus) • BPPV: no imaging or vestibular testing if criteria are met • Ménière’s: salt restriction, diuretics, then intratympanic therapy • Avoid routine vestibular suppressants (meclizine, benzodiazepines) beyond the first days • Fatigue • Not a single mechanism: central (cytokines IL-1/TNF-α signalling, neuroendocrine and sleep dysregulation), peripheral (muscle energy, anaemia, hypoxia) and psychological contributors overlap. • Common substrates: depression/anxiety, sleep disorders, endocrine, anaemia, infection, cardiopulmonary, renal/hepatic disease, malignancy, drugs, post-infectious states. • Fever, night sweats, unexplained weight loss • Lymphadenopathy or organomegaly • Objective muscle weakness or fatigable weakness (ptosis, diplopia) • Dyspnoea on exertion, chest pain, syncope • Suicidal thoughts • Focal neurological signs • New drug started or alcohol/substance misuse • Screen mood/anxiety (PHQ-9/GAD-7), sleep history (STOP-BANG), medication review • Distinguish breakaway (effort-related) weakness from true weakness • Limited first-line: CBC with differential, electrolytes incl. calcium, glucose, renal, liver, TSH • Add ferritin, HbA1c, ESR/CRP, HIV/hepatitis, cortisol only if indicated • Overnight polysomnography if apnoea suspected • Avoid broad unfocused testing, routine ANA and whole-body imaging • Treat the underlying cause first • CBT and graded activity adapted to the individual (note: NICE 2021 advises caution with graded exercise in ME/CFS — pacing-based approach) • Prior-knowledge note: NICE NG206 (2021) ME/CFS guidance shifted away from GET/curative CBT — verify before applying to ME/CFS. • Weakness & Paralysis • UMN lesion (cortex → corticospinal/bulbospinal) → decreased drive to LMNs: spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski, weakness of extensors in arms and flexors in legs. • LMN lesion (anterior horn, root, plexus, nerve) → atrophy, fasciculations, hypotonia, hyporeflexia in a segmental or nerve distribution. • Acute onset (stroke window) • Rapidly ascending weakness, areflexia, breathing or bulbar difficulty • Spinal level with bladder/bowel loss (cord/cauda equina) • Saddle anaesthesia • Fever with back pain and weakness • Respiratory muscle involvement • Pattern: hemiparesis, paraparesis, quadriparesis, monoparesis, distal, proximal • Tone, bulk, fasciculations, reflexes, plantar response, sensory level • Table 24-1 sign comparison (UMN / LMN / myopathic / psychogenic) • Hoover sign / give-way for functional weakness • Acute hemiparesis: emergent CT/CTA or MRI brain • Paraparesis: urgent MRI spine • LMN/myopathic: CK, electrolytes, TSH, EMG/NCS • Suspected MG: AChR/MuSK antibodies, repetitive nerve stimulation, chest CT • Stroke: reperfusion pathways per local protocol • Cord compression: urgent decompression ± steroids per aetiology • GBS: IVIG or plasma exchange, monitor respiratory function • MG: cholinesterase inhibitors, immunotherapy, thymectomy where indicated • Use Harrison Fig 24-3 algorithm: localise first, then imaging/EMG. Check local stroke and GBS guidelines for current treatment windows. • Numbness, Tingling & Sensory Loss • Positive symptoms (paraesthesia, dysaesthesia, pain) vs negative (numbness, hypoaesthesia, anaesthesia). Distribution identifies the lesion: nerve, root, plexus, cord, brainstem, thalamus, cortex. • Patterns: stocking-glove (length-dependent neuropathy), dermatomal (root), dissociated loss (syringomyelia), crossed (lateral medulla), hemisensory (thalamus). • Sensory level with weakness or sphincter dysfunction • Rapidly progressive course • Saddle numbness • Hemisensory loss of sudden onset • Lhermitte sign with myelopathy • Pain/temp (pinprick), light touch, vibration (128 Hz), joint position, Romberg • Neuropathy: glucose/HbA1c, B12 (± MMA), TSH, SPEP/immunofixation, renal, liver, HIV • MRI spine/brain for central localisation • Consider paraneoplastic/autoimmune panels if subacute sensory neuronopathy • Treat cause (glycaemic control, B12 replacement, stop toxin) • Foot care and fall prevention in sensory loss • For painful neuropathy follow current AAN/EFNS-style first-line drug classes (gabapentinoids, SNRI, TCA) — verify with local formulary. • Gait, Imbalance & Falls • Patterns: cautious, spastic, parkinsonian/freezing, frontal (magnetic), cerebellar (wide base), sensory (stamping, worse in dark), neuromuscular (steppage), functional. • Normal pressure hydrocephalus: gait apraxia, cognitive decline, incontinence. • Fall with syncope or injury • Head strike on anticoagulant • ≥2 falls in 12 months • Acute gait change with focal signs • Rapidly progressive gait failure • New incontinence with cognitive change (NPH) • Orthostatic BP, vision, feet, cognition, medication review (sedatives, antihypertensives, anticholinergics) • Home/environment review • B12, TSH, glucose, renal, vitamin D if indicated • Bone health (DXA) after fall • Multifactorial intervention in high-risk patients: reduce culprit medications, exercise (balance and strength, Tai Chi), vision correction, footwear, home modification • Physiotherapy and assistive devices • Confusion & Delirium • Predisposition (dementia, age, sensory impairment) × precipitant (infection, drugs, metabolic, surgery, ICU) — a ‘stress test for the brain’. • Medications (anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, opioids) and alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal are common causes. • Severe agitation endangering self • Fever with neck stiffness (meningitis/encephalitis) • Focal deficits or head trauma • Hypoxia, hypoglycaemia, sepsis • Alcohol withdrawal (autonomic instability, seizures) • Seizure or suspected non-convulsive status • Thiamine deficiency (ataxia, ophthalmoplegia) • Neurological exam for focal signs, asterixis • CBC, electrolytes (Na, Ca, Mg), glucose, renal, liver, ± ammonia • Urinalysis/culture, chest X-ray, blood cultures, ECG, oxygen saturation/ABG • Drug/toxicology screen in younger patients • Second tier: B12, thiamine, TSH, cortisol, ANA, HIV, autoimmune encephalitis panel • Non-drug care: reorientation, glasses/hearing aids, sleep–wake cycle, mobilisation, hydration, avoid restraints and catheters • Give thiamine before glucose in at-risk patients • Prevent with multicomponent programmes (HELP model) • Coma • Coma: deep unarousable unresponsiveness with eyes closed. Related: stupor, obtundation, vegetative state (wakeful unresponsiveness), minimally conscious state, locked-in syndrome, akinetic mutism, catatonia, brain death. • Arousal depends on the brainstem reticular activating system and thalamic projections to both hemispheres. • GCS ≤8 or falling • Unequal or fixed pupils • Posturing, Cushing response • Hypoglycaemia, hypoxia, opioid toxidrome • Fever with meningism • Head or neck trauma • Anticoagulant use • Neck exam only after cervical injury considered • Point-of-care glucose, ABG, electrolytes, renal, liver, ammonia, toxicology, ECG • EEG for non-convulsive status or unexplained coma • Raised ICP: head elevation, hyperosmolar therapy, neurosurgical referral, avoid hypotonic fluids • Specific: reverse anticoagulation, treat Wernicke, correct metabolic derangement • Prognosis and brain-death determination per current national criteria (e.g., 2023 AAN/AAP/CNS/SCCM consensus) • Prior-knowledge note: 2023 AAN/AAP/CNS/SCCM brain death/death by neurologic criteria guideline — verify with local legal requirements. • mido • name • Alpha-1 agonist • generic • Midodrine • items • brand • Actiful • company • Tas Med India • Cipmido • Cipla • Hypodrin • Alniche Life Sciences • Midorise • Torrent • Midodrive • Sun Pharma • note • fludro • Mineralocorticoid • Fludrocortisone • Floricot • Samarth Life Sciences • drox • Noradrenaline precursor • Droxidopa • No five India-market brands verified. https://motion-sickness-clinical-guide.v.text: MotionCare | Motion sickness clinical guide ≈ MotionCare CLINICAL COMPANION · INDIA Print / save PDF CONSULTATION WORKSPACE 01 Assessment 02 Tests & differentials 03 Treatment 04 Indian medicines 05 Follow-up 06 Sources Evidence reviewed 1 November 2026 Clinician decision support. Verify the patient, product and prescription. TRAVEL HEALTH / VESTIBULAR CARE Steadier journeys. Better clinical decisions. Assess motion-linked symptoms, identify when to investigate, and plan prevention with an India-focused medicine reference. Assessment → plan 15 Indian brand references No patient data stored For clinician use. New neurological symptoms, collapse or severe dehydration require urgent assessment. This app does not diagnose or issue prescriptions. 01 / ASSESSMENT Start with the pattern Reset assessment Patient & journey Age in years Consultation Before travel / prevention Symptoms now / acute care Travel duration 6 hours or less More than 6 hours Symptom impact Mild — can function Moderate — limits activity Severe — disabling symptoms Symptoms occur with vehicle travel, VR or visual motion Similar previous episodes Symptoms at rest / persist after motion stops New hearing loss, tinnitus or ear symptoms Safety screen Warning signs New weakness, double vision, speech difficulty, severe sudden headache or unable to walk Collapse, chest pain or altered consciousness Cannot retain fluids, very low urine output or blood in vomit Pregnant or breastfeeding Glaucoma / urinary retention Parkinsonism Kidney / liver impairment Alcohol, sedatives, QT drugs or other antihistamines Driving or safety-critical duties Generate assessment & next steps → Rule-based checklist, not a validated severity score. No information is transmitted or retained. 02 / INVESTIGATIONS Test the clinical concern Typical episodes: no routine tests A recurrent pattern of nausea, pallor or sweating during travel, resolving after exposure, is usually assessed clinically. Do not order routine CT, MRI or vestibular testing for this pattern alone. Examine first Check vitals and hydration; consider orthostatic BP. Examine gait, eye movements, neurological signs and hearing when symptoms are atypical. Review migraine, medicines and pregnancy possibility. HINTS is for trained clinicians evaluating the appropriate acute vestibular syndrome; it is not a self-test or a general motion sickness screen. Selective tests Repeated vomiting / dehydration: electrolytes, renal function and glucose as indicated. Pregnancy test when clinically relevant, with consent. Palpitations, syncope or QT-risk medicines: ECG as indicated. Hearing changes: audiometry / ENT review. Suspected central disease: urgent stroke / neurology pathway; imaging chosen by the evaluating team. These are clinician-selected investigations for alternative diagnoses or complications, not a mandatory panel. Differential guide Pattern Consider Next step Brief spinning on turning in bed BPPV Appropriate positional examination Recurrent dizziness with migraine features Vestibular migraine Clinical migraine assessment Continuous new vertigo / gait impairment Peripheral or central vestibular disease Urgent assessment if severe or new Persistent rocking after a voyage Mal de débarquement syndrome Vestibular specialist review if persistent 03 / MANAGEMENT Prevention comes first Before the journey Sleep adequately, avoid alcohol and choose a seat with less movement: near aircraft wings or the middle of a ship. Keep the head supported; look towards a stable distant view. Avoid reading and screens. During symptoms Reduce or stop the provoking activity safely, get fresh air, rest and use small frequent sips of fluid / ORS. Ongoing vomiting may prevent oral absorption; clinician-directed treatment and hydration may be needed. Ginger has uncertain benefit; acupressure bands have not reliably outperformed placebo. Adult reference only. Select one suitable agent after checking contraindications and the local label. Do not combine sedating drugs or add single ingredients already present in a fixed combination. No driving or alcohol. Medication reference Agent Adult reference / timing Key precautions Meclizine 25–50 mg orally before exposure; allow around 2 hours for onset. Repeat only according to the specific local label. Sedation, dry mouth; review anticholinergic risks. Dimenhydrinate 50–100 mg orally; allow around 2 hours for onset. Follow product-specific repeat interval and daily maximum. Sedation and additive effects with other antihistamines. Promethazine 25 mg orally may be considered by a clinician for intense exposure; onset about 2 hours. Follow local label. Marked sedation; contraindicated below 2 years. No injection self-use. Cinnarizine NHS 15 mg formulation: 30 mg 2 hours before travel, then 15 mg every 8 hours if needed. Indian 25/75 mg products are not tablet-for-tablet equivalents of this regimen. Check local product instructions. Review Parkinsonism. Scopolamine / hyoscine hydrobromide Adult patch delivering 1 mg over 72 hours; allow 6–8 hours before exposure. Follow the exact product label. Do not cut or double patches. Avoid in children, glaucoma or urinary retention; review heat-related adverse effects. Indian supply not verified. CDC dose / onset overview and NHS cinnarizine guidance. Onset estimates do not replace manufacturer directions. Review prescription frequency, maximum dose and duration before use. Spinfree & similar combinations Spinfree contains cinnarizine 20 mg + dimenhydrinate 40 mg. The Indian prescribing information indicates treatment of vertigo, so this app does not automatically recommend it for uncomplicated motion sickness. For clinician reference, its vertigo label uses one tablet three times daily after food for no more than four weeks. Avoid in severe renal impairment (CrCl <25 mL/min), severe hepatic disease, angle-closure glaucoma or urinary retention. Pregnancy safety is not established; avoid during breastfeeding. Not a pediatric travel regimen. Check the full label and interactions. Read Spinfree prescribing information ↗ Medicines that do not replace vestibular prevention Ondansetron and newer non-sedating antihistamines are ineffective for motion sickness. Betahistine and pregnancy nausea combinations are not default travel-sickness treatments. Stimulants are not recommended to counteract sedation. Special populations Children, pregnant or breastfeeding patients, older adults and people with significant comorbidities need individualized review. The app deliberately generates no pediatric or pregnancy prescription. 04 / INDIAN MEDICINE DIRECTORY Know the ingredient. Then check the brand. Five references per listed group, including Spinfree. Cinnarizine also has H1 activity; the groups below organize the directory rather than imply entirely separate mechanisms. Search brands, ingredients or company Group All groups Antimuscarinic availability gap Five Indian motion-sickness brands of scopolamine / hyoscine hydrobromide could not be verified. No invented brands are included. Hyoscine butylbromide (such as abdominal antispasmodic products) is not a substitute. Prices and stock change; use each linked listing for the current pack price. Retail listing evidence is separate from clinical treatment evidence. 05 / REASSESSMENT Close the loop After an episode Confirm improvement once the provoking motion ends. Check hydration, intake and urine output after vomiting. Review sedation, blurred vision, confusion, urinary difficulty or abnormal movements. Arrange review for persistent symptoms, new susceptibility or recurrence without travel. Before the next journey Record trigger, duration and functional impact. Review which positioning measures helped. Check medicine, dose, timing and adverse effects with the clinician. Discuss a supervised suitability check / trial before travel where appropriate; do not drive during a trial. Consider vestibular / migraine evaluation for atypical recurrent episodes. Escalate immediately New neurological symptoms, collapse, severe headache, inability to walk, blood in vomit or severe dehydration need urgent assessment. Sudden hearing loss also needs prompt care. 06 / EVIDENCE & PROVENANCE Sources you can inspect Clinical content is an original summary based on the supplied PDF, current public guidance and product labels. https://palpitation-hazel.vercel.app/.text: Palpitations Assessment Clinical decision support Palpitations Assessment Based on Harrison’s Ch.43 (Loscalzo), updated with guideline evidence Assess Causes Manage Learn Evidence Patient Age (y) HR (/min) SBP (mmHg) 1. Red flags (haemodynamic compromise) − Harrison: the principal goal is to determine whether the symptom is caused by a life-threatening arrhythmia. Hypotension, shock or altered consciousness now red flag Syncope with the palpitations red flag Ischaemic-type chest pain with palpitations red flag Signs of heart failure / pulmonary oedema red flag Presyncope / lightheadedness concern Dyspnoea with palpitations concern 2. Onset / offset − Sudden onset and sudden termination Gradual onset and gradual fade 3. Rhythm the patient feels (ask them to tap it out) − Regular and rapid Irregular / chaotic Isolated skipped / missing beats or a thump Forceful pounding at a normal-ish rate Slow beats or pauses concern 4. Duration of episodes + 5. Distinguishing features + 6. Triggers and context + 7. Associated symptoms + 8. Cardiac history and risk + 9. Examination + 10. ECG / rhythm strip findings + Reset Select findings above — the assessment updates live. Monitor selector How often do episodes occur? Daily Weekly Monthly Rarer Extended patch monitor or external loop/event recorder (1–2 weeks) 2-week ambulatory ECG has the best yield-to-cost for unexplained palpitations (AAFP 2024). Event recorders yield more diagnoses than 48-h Holter in palpitations (controlled trial, Ann Intern Med 1996). Ask the patient to keep a diary or press the event marker during symptoms — Harrison stresses this is essential for interpretation. Educational decision support for clinicians. https://diabetes-clinical-care.vercel.ap.text: Diabetes in Clinical Care Diabetes in Clinical Care Based on Harrison's Principles, Ch.403-406 (Diagnosis, Management, Complications, Hypoglycemia) Knowledge Base Assessment Pathophysiology Investigations Treatment Complications Prevention Complication Dx & Tx Indian Medicines 2026 Updates Case Studies Quiz Definition & burden DM is a group of metabolic disorders sharing hyperglycemia, from reduced insulin secretion, decreased glucose utilization and increased glucose production. Leading cause of ESRD, non-traumatic amputation and adult blindness; raises CVD risk. Global: 463 M (2019) rising to 642 M by 2040; about 50% undiagnosed. Glucose homeostasis Fasting: low insulin + modest glucagon drive gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis; glucose uptake by muscle/fat falls. Fed: insulin rises, glucagon falls; muscle is the main site of postprandial uptake. Insulin: proinsulin cleaved to insulin + C-peptide; C-peptide marks endogenous secretion. Incretins (GLP-1, GIP) amplify glucose-dependent insulin secretion and suppress glucagon. Classification (etiologic) Type 1: immune-mediated beta-cell destruction. Type 2: insulin resistance with relative insulin secretory defect. Specific types: MODY and monogenic, neonatal DM, exocrine pancreas disease, endocrinopathies, drug-induced, infections. Gestational DM (GDM). Atypical forms Ketosis-prone T2DM (often African American or Asian): DKA at onset, later controlled with oral agents. Latent autoimmune diabetes of adult (5-10% phenotypic T2DM with GAD/ICA antibodies): likely to need insulin within 5 years. Educational reference for clinicians. With raised enzymes, R at least 5 suggests hepatocellular injury, R at most 2 suggests cholestatic injury, and intermediate values suggest mixed injury. This does not establish the cause. Artificial and non-sugar sweeteners Non-sugar sweeteners activate sweet-taste receptors (T1R2/T1R3) with little or no glycaemic carbohydrate contribution. They are not essential nutrients and should not replace a balanced dietary pattern. Type Mechanism / use India brand examples* Clinical caution Sucralose (INS 955) High-intensity chlorinated sucrose derivative; negligible calories at typical doses Sugar Free Natura Check product ingredients and bulking agents; avoid assuming weight-loss benefit Aspartame (INS 951) Peptide sweetener, metabolised to amino acids; intense sweetness at low doses Equal (verify local formulation) Contraindicated in phenylketonuria; label warning Steviol glycosides (INS 960) Stevia-derived sweet-taste receptor agonists Sugar Free Green, Zevic (check variant) Natural origin does not imply proven cardiovascular benefit Saccharin (INS 954) High-intensity non-nutritive sweetener Sweetex (check India availability) Read label and follow FSSAI permitted uses Acesulfame-K (INS 950) High-intensity sweetener often blended with others Found in some packaged zero-sugar products; verify label Check combined sweeteners on ingredient list Polyols (erythritol, xylitol, sorbitol) Sugar alcohols; variable energy and glycaemic effect; distinct from WHO NSS category Ingredient-dependent Indian retail products May cause GI symptoms; cardiovascular outcome evidence remains uncertain *Brand examples are illustrative, not endorsements; formulations and Indian availability require verification against the current pack. Clinical recommendations Prefer unsweetened drinks and gradual reduction in overall sweetness. WHO 2023 conditionally advises against using non-sugar sweeteners for long-term weight control or NCD prevention; people with pre-existing diabetes are outside this recommendation's scope. For diabetes, replacing sugar may reduce immediate carbohydrate intake, but assess the whole food, glucose response and nutritional quality. Check FSSAI label requirements, especially phenylketonuria warnings for aspartame and child-related warnings. Pregnancy, children and complex chronic disease require individualised dietary advice. Placebo-subtracted loss 2.1% (6.4 vs 4.4%) over 24 weeks. No increased safety risks. • Intragastric balloons REHAPE, ORBERA (endoscopic) and OBALON (swallowed). Approved for up to 6 months in BMI 30–40. 6-month loss 9.7% (5.6% control-subtracted). Adverse: nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain. • BMI classes (Table 402-1) Class BMI Disease risk Underweight — Healthy 18.5–24.9 — Overweight 25–29.9 Increased Obesity I 30–34.9 High Obesity II 35–39.9 Very high Obesity III ≥40 Extremely high • Sleep and stress Short sleep is linked to metabolic change, appetite dysregulation, sympathetic overactivity and insulin sensitivity changes. Stress may raise cortisol through adrenal-cortical activation. • Established cardiovascular disease • Moderate-severe obstructive sleep apnea • mash • MASH with stage 2–3 fibrosis • Migraine • Smoker, untreated depression or alcohol use disorder • cost • Cost or coverage barrier • oral • Prefers an oral drug • Pregnant, lactating or planning pregnancy • Severe IBD or gastroparesis • panc • History of pancreatitis • Coronary disease, uncontrolled hypertension, hyperthyroidism, glaucoma, MAOI use or substance use disorder • Seizure disorder, bulimia, chronic opioid use or severe renal/hepatic disease • Established CVD: subcutaneous semaglutide has proven CV benefit with or without diabetes (SELECT: events 6.5% vs 8%). Tirzepatide and liraglutide have proof only with diabetes. • OSA: tirzepatide is approved for moderate-severe OSA with obesity. • Diabetes: tirzepatide has the greatest glycemic efficacy. Reduce insulin or sulfonylurea dose in the first 4 weeks and self-monitor glucose daily during titration. • Cost: generic semaglutide is now sold in India. Do not use compounded products. If no GLP-1 agent is accessible, use the alternatives below. • GLP-1 agents not suitable ( • medullary thyroid cancer/MEN2 history • ].filter(Boolean).join( • ). Use an alternative. • Phentermine-topiramate is the preferred non-GLP-1 option (best for a goal within 10–15% of weight). If cost is the barrier, generic phentermine and topiramate can be given separately (off-label, efficacy and safety not established). • Phentermine-topiramate is contraindicated by the ticked conditions (CHD, uncontrolled HTN, hyperthyroidism, glaucoma, MAOI within 14 days, substance use disorder, pregnancy). • Migraine: topiramate also prevents migraine, favoring phentermine-topiramate. • Avoid with the seizure/bulimia/opioid history ticked. • % meets the ≥4–5% benchmark at 12 weeks on the maximum tolerated dose. Continue, long term if well tolerated. • Below 4–5% after 12 weeks at the maximum tolerated dose: usually stop and try another agent. Exceptions: progressive weight gain that stopped on treatment, or a comorbidity such as OSA that improved. Partial response: add a drug from another class (off-label). • Agent selector Uses the Assess tab answers for thyroid cancer history. Tick all that apply. Based on UpToDate (2026): GLP-1-based agents are preferred. • Candidates for drug therapy • Failed comprehensive lifestyle plus BMI ≥30, or BMI 27–29.9 with ≥1 comorbidity, or central adiposity with ≥1 comorbidity. Lower threshold for Asian patients because BMI alone underestimates risk (candidates indication eligible asian south asian). • Waist circumference • Obesity staging • Evaluation steps • Four steps: focused history (diet, activity, sleep, stress), physical exam, comorbidity assessment, readiness assessment. Use neutral words such as weight or BMI. Fasting lipids, chemistry, HbA1c and blood pressure for all. • Secondary and drug-induced obesity • Consider PCOS, hypothyroidism, Cushing, hypothalamic disease. Weight-gaining drugs: insulin, sulfonylureas, thiazolidinediones, steroids, clozapine, olanzapine, risperidone, lithium, tricyclics, MAOIs, paroxetine, mirtazapine, valproate, gabapentin, carbamazepine. • Readiness to change • Motivational interviewing with 0–10 importance and confidence scale. Readiness is motivation versus resistance. Assess stressors, psychiatric status, time and expectations. • Lifestyle: diet • Lifestyle: activity and behavior • Goals of drug treatment • Optimize lifestyle, baseline nutrition assessment, treat comorbidities (OSA, hypothyroidism), minimize weight-promoting medicines, counsel: drugs vary in response, plateau is expected, stopping causes regain. • Dual GLP-1/GIP agonist (brands Mounjaro, Yurpeak). 2.5 mg weekly ×4 weeks, increase by 2.5 mg every ≥4 weeks to max 15 mg. SURMOUNT-1: −15%, −19.5%, −20.9% at 72 weeks. Approved for moderate-severe OSA and type 2 diabetes. Slower titration with retinopathy. • Oral semaglutide 25 mg daily, empty stomach with ≤120 mL water, wait 30 minutes. Orforglipron 0.8 to 17.2 mg daily, no food restriction, CYP3A4 interactions. Efficacy −13.6% (oral semaglutide) and −11.2% (orforglipron). • 3 mg daily, titrate weekly from 0.6 mg. About −4.7% versus placebo. Continue if ≥4% loss by 16 weeks. CV benefit only at 1.8 mg in diabetes. • Contraindicated in pregnancy and with personal or family history of medullary thyroid cancer or MEN2. Avoid severe IBD or gastroparesis, lactation. Caution with pancreatitis history. Avoid compounded products. No calcitonin screening. • Nausea 25–40%, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation 10–20%, mostly with dose escalation. Smaller slow meals, avoid fatty food, delay escalation, or switch GLP-1 agent. Rare gallbladder disease, pancreatitis, obstruction. Hold or adjust before anesthesia. • For patients without CVD or uncontrolled HTN with goal 10–15%. 3.75/23 ×14 d, 7.5/46, up to 15/92. Teratogenic (orofacial clefts): monthly pregnancy tests. Dry mouth, constipation, paresthesia. Taper to avoid seizures. Check bicarbonate and creatinine. REMS. • 8/90 mg tablets, up to 2 tablets twice daily. 4–5% more loss than placebo. Nausea 30%. Avoid with seizures, bulimia, opioids, uncontrolled hypertension. Monitor suicidality. Suits smokers, depression, alcohol use disorder. CV safety uncertain. • Second-line. 120 mg tid with meals blocks 25–30% of dietary fat. GI effects 15–30%, fat-soluble vitamin loss (give multivitamin), oxalate kidney injury, warfarin interaction. Avoid in malabsorption, cholestasis, pregnancy. • Dietary supplements (hidden drugs such as sibutramine), hCG diet, calcium. Withdrawn: lorcaserin (cancer signal), sibutramine, rimonabant, fen-phen. • Long-term therapy needed. Regain about 0.4 kg per month after stopping. Tirzepatide maintenance 52 weeks: −21.9% (10–15 mg) vs −16.6% (5 mg) vs −9.9% (placebo). Orforglipron after tirzepatide or semaglutide kept 75–80% of loss. • Special populations • Post-bariatric regain: semaglutide 2.4 mg −18% vs +0.4%. Postpartum: start after lactation. Antipsychotic obesity: GLP-1 or metformin, avoid phentermine. Monogenic or hypothalamic obesity: setmelanotide. • Tirzepatide: Mounjaro (Lilly), Yurpeak (Cipla). Semaglutide: Wegovy, Poviztra (Emcure), Ozempic (diabetes), generics Noveltreat (Sun), Semaglyn (Zydus) since patent expiry on 20 March 2026. https://antibiotics-guid-clay.vercel.app.text: Antimicrobial Use Guide — ICMR 2019 EMC Digitals · Clinical Reference Antimicrobial Use in Common Syndromes Empiric and directed antibiotic therapy, curated from the ICMR Treatment Guidelines for Antimicrobial Use in Common Syndromes, 2nd Edition (2019). Search syndromes, organisms or drugs 2 . Acute Undifferentiated Fever & Tropical Infections 3 . Sepsis & Septic Shock 4 . Respiratory Tract Infections & Community-Acquired Pneumonia 5 . Intra-Abdominal Infections, SBP & Acute Diarrhea 6 . Skin & Soft Tissue Infections 7 . Bone & Joint Infections 8 . CNS Infections 9 . Urinary Tract Infections 10 . Hospital-Acquired Infections 12 . Pelvic / Obstetric & Gynaecological Infections 13 . Infective Endocarditis 2 . Acute Undifferentiated Fever & Tropical Infections Community-onset fever in adults, malaria, dengue, scrub typhus, typhoid, leptospirosis and rickettsial disease. ICMR Guidelines 2019, pp. 5-28 Typhoid fever Salmonella Typhi / Paratyphi A Preferred Oral: Cotrimoxazole or Azithromycin. Parenteral: Ceftriaxone Alternative Cefixime, Chloramphenicol, Ciprofloxacin Duration: 10-14 days Change empiric regimen based on susceptibility. Quinolone resistance up to 69% in S. Typhi. Empiric therapy for suspected Gram-positive infection S. pneumoniae, S. pyogenes, S. aureus Preferred Cefazolin or Cloxacillin Alternative Amoxicillin-clavulanate, or Vancomycin (if anaphylactic penicillin allergy or MRSA possible) Adjust after culture and susceptibility data. Empiric therapy for suspected Gram-negative infection (e.g. pyelonephritis, intra-abdominal infection) E. coli, K. pneumoniae, anaerobes (esp. Bacteroides in IAI) Preferred Piperacillin-tazobactam or Cefoperazone-sulbactam Alternative Imipenem, Meropenem, or Ertapenem (carbapenems preferred if more seriously ill) Separate anaerobic coverage unnecessary for IAI when using BL-BLIs or carbapenems. De-escalate to ciprofloxacin/cotrimoxazole/3rd gen cephalosporin if sensitive. Rickettsial infection / Scrub typhus Orientia tsutsugamushi, Rickettsia conorii, R. typhi Preferred Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily (oral or IV) for 7 days (up to 15 days) Alternative Chloramphenicol 500 mg qid (7 days adults) or 150 mg/kg/day (5 days children); Rifampicin/azithromycin/clarithromycin in doxycycline-resistant strains Duration: 7 days Rifampicin monotherapy strongly discouraged in TB-endemic settings such as India. Leptospirosis Preferred Penicillin G or Doxycycline Alternative Ceftriaxone Duration: 7 days Vivax malaria P. vivax Preferred Oral Chloroquine, followed by Primaquine (0.25 mg/kg/day for 14 days) Alternative Artemether-lumefantrine Falciparum malaria — uncomplicated P. falciparum Preferred Able to take orally: Oral Artesunate + Sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (SP) for 3 days (except NE states: Artemether-lumefantrine); all mixed infections get full ACT course + primaquine 0.25 mg/kg/day x 14 days Alternative Artemether-lumefantrine; Unable to take orally: IV Artesunate, switch to oral ASAP Severe / complicated malaria Preferred IV/IM Artesunate 2.4 mg/kg (3 mg/kg if <20 kg) at 0, 12, 24 h then every 24 h until oral tolerated, min 24 h, then complete 3-day oral ACT Alternative Artemether IM 3.2 mg/kg loading, 1.6 mg/kg/day maintenance, if artesunate unavailable Parenteral artesunate is treatment of choice — substantial mortality reduction vs quinine. Cholera-related severe dengue / acute febrile illness (empiric) Preferred Doxycycline may be considered empirically if RDTs for malaria and dengue are negative Dengue itself needs no antibiotics — supportive fluid management per WHO grading. https://wide-qrs-tachycardia.vercel.app/.text: Wide QRS Lab | EMC ∿ Wide QRS Lab by EMC · Clinical learning workspace 12-LEAD ECG WORKSPACE 01 Analyze rhythm 02 Learn the criteria 03 ECG image atlas 04 References & scope Stability does not exclude VT. When a wide-complex rhythm remains uncertain, manage as VT and seek expert help. Miller et al., 2006 RHYTHM INTERPRETATION / ADULTS Analyze wide QRS tachycardia Work through clinical context and ECG findings. Every conclusion shows its supporting criteria. Clinician learning and decision support. Enter observed findings; this app does not automatically interpret ECG images. Do not delay emergency care. 1 Clinical context Pulse Unknown / not assessed Present Absent Clinical stability Unknown / not assessed Stable Hypotension, shock, altered mentation, ischemic pain or acute HF Heart rate (bpm) QRS duration (ms) Rhythm regularity Unknown Regular Irregular QRS morphology Unknown Monomorphic, RBBB-like Monomorphic, LBBB-like Monomorphic, other Polymorphic 2 ECG criteria Use “unknown” when the finding cannot be assessed. Absence of VT features does not exclude VT. 3 Alternative mechanisms Review an ECG locally PNG, JPG or WebP · stays in your browser · no automatic image diagnosis Remove ECG Analyze entered findings → Reset INTERPRETATION Start with the patient Assess pulse and clinical stability, then enter the ECG findings. ∿∿∿ The Brugada sequence applies to regular, monomorphic WCT. Other mechanisms require a separate differential. At the bedside Assess pulse, perfusion and stability. Obtain a 12-lead ECG and compare a baseline tracing. Look for AV dissociation, capture and fusion. Assess morphology and alternative causes. Review criteria → Choose a condition The diagnostic criteria Brugada sequence For regular monomorphic wide-complex tachycardia: no RS in any chest lead → RS interval >100 ms in any chest lead → AV dissociation → morphology compatible with VT in V1/V2 and V6. A positive step favors VT; stop at the first positive step. Only when every step is confidently negative does the algorithm favor SVT with aberrancy. Unknown findings leave the sequence incomplete. Pre-excitation, pacing, drug effects and baseline conduction disease can confound it. Original figures from your supplied article. Select a figure to enlarge it and review its teaching point. Primary learning source Miller JM, Das MK, Yadav AV, Bhakta D, Nair G, Alberte C. Value of the 12-Lead ECG in Wide QRS Tachycardia. Cardiology Clinics. 2006;24:439–451. Figures 1–9 are extracted from the user-supplied “ECG VT 1.pdf.” Copyright remains with the original rights holders. ECG examples are teaching material, not patient-specific evidence. Contemporary emergency reference AHA 2025 Adult Advanced Life Support — sections 15–16 ↗ Emergency prompts use this reference; the 2006 article is used for diagnostic teaching. Checked 30 September 2026. Scope and limitations No AI image classifier, probability estimate, validated clinical score or automated ECG measurement. Rules depend on clinician-entered findings and cannot establish a definitive diagnosis. Brugada criteria are limited to regular monomorphic WCT; missing information never becomes a negative finding. No patient identifiers are requested. Uploaded images remain in browser memory and are cleared on refresh. Drug dosing and individualized prescribing are outside this app’s scope. Use local resuscitation protocols and specialist review. The article does not include a dedicated polymorphic VT/torsades tracing; the app explicitly identifies this image gap. Each has LBBB-like and RBBB-like V1/V6 examples. • Precordial concordance • Capture and fusion beats • V1 and V6 morphology • Compare typical aberrancy with VT patterns in RBBB-like and LBBB-like tachycardias. Assess both leads, not only QRS width. • Unusual V1 configurations • Rs and W configurations illustrated in the article favor VT over conventional aberrancy. Baseline disease and pre-excitation need separate assessment. • Why the V6 R/S ratio matters • Absent RS — an important exception • The article includes VT examples and a bottom-panel LBBB SVT example with no precordial RS. This criterion is not perfectly specific. • Alternans can occur in VT • Beat-to-beat QRS amplitude variation is not a reliable distinction between VT and SVT. This tracing shows alternans during VT. • Ventricular tachycardia • VENTRICULAR ORIGIN • Ventricular activation may proceed through myocardium instead of normal His–Purkinje conduction. Structural heart disease raises suspicion, but idiopathic VT can occur in a normal heart. • True capture or fusion beats. • A stable patient can still have sustained VT. A 1:1 VA relationship does not exclude VT. • SVT with aberrancy • SUPRAVENTRICULAR ORIGIN • An atrial or AV-junctional tachycardia is conducted with pre-existing or rate-related bundle branch block. AVNRT, orthodromic AVRT, atrial tachycardia and flutter can all appear wide when aberrancy is present. • Typical RBBB: often rsR′ in V1 and a dominant R with terminal S in V6. • An identical baseline QRS supports aberrancy, with exceptions including bundle branch reentry VT. • Rate near 150 bpm may prompt a search for flutter, but rate alone cannot classify WCT. • Pre-excited tachycardia • ACCESSORY PATHWAY • Figure 2, third column, illustrates pre-excitation in V1/V6. • Pre-excitation can mimic VT morphology, so VT-versus-aberrancy rules do not establish the mechanism. • Abnormal baseline QRS • BASELINE CONDUCTION DISEASE • Cardiomyopathy or repaired congenital heart disease can produce unusual baseline activation. A supraventricular rhythm may retain this broad, atypical QRS. • Figure 2, fourth column, shows abnormal baseline QRS examples. • Compare a prior 12-lead ECG at baseline. • A matching QRS supports a baseline conduction mechanism but does not prove SVT. • A narrower QRS during tachycardia or contralateral BBB can favor VT, with conduction-delay exceptions. • Drug / electrolyte widening • REVERSIBLE CONTRIBUTORS • Hyperkalemia, acidosis and sodium-channel-blocking drug effects can widen an otherwise supraventricular rhythm. These conditions may also provoke ventricular arrhythmia. • Figure 2, fifth column, shows nonspecific widening examples, not a diagnosis of a particular toxin. • Review potassium, renal function, acid-base status and medications or exposure history. • QRS-duration thresholds lose specificity when drug or metabolic effects are present. • Ventricular pacing • DEVICE-RELATED RHYTHM • Ventricular pacing produces a wide QRS and may track atrial tachycardia or occur during device-mediated tachycardia. Patients with a device can also develop independent VT. • Figure 2, rightmost column, shows ventricular-paced V1/V6 examples. • Compare prior paced morphology and arrange device interrogation. • The presence of a pacemaker does not establish that a wide tachycardia is paced. • Polymorphic VT / torsades • EMERGENCY DIFFERENTIAL • Sustained polymorphic VT requires immediate unsynchronized shock under AHA 2025 guidance. • Do not apply Brugada morphology criteria or give adenosine to polymorphic WCT. • Review baseline QT, potassium, magnesium and QT-prolonging medicines. • No dedicated polymorphic VT or torsades ECG is supplied in this PDF. The monomorphic examples must not be relabeled as torsades. • capture • True capture or fusion beats • noRS • No RS complex in any of V1–V6 • axis • Extreme right-superior QRS axis • concordance • All chest leads predominantly same polarity • baseline • QRS identical to baseline tracing • preexcitation • Accessory pathway / pre-excitation suspected • pacing • Ventricular pacing suspected • metabolic • Drug or electrolyte widening suspected • notice • P waves march independently of QRS complexes. Absence of visible dissociation is common and does not rule out VT. A 1:1 atrioventricular relationship can occur during VT. • Capture & fusion • Identify atrial timing and a true captured or hybrid complex. Premature beats, variable aberrancy and pre-excitation may mimic these appearances. • RBBB-like morphology • LBBB-like morphology • Duration and axis • Concordance • Brugada RS criteria • Baseline comparison and alternans • Identical baseline morphology supports aberrancy but does not exclude bundle branch reentry VT. Alternans and normal blood pressure cannot reliably classify the rhythm. • #lesson-cards • Work through clinical context and ECG findings. ECG diagnosis Holter report Image library Learning hub Knowledge base References ECG findings QRS Narrow (≤120 ms) Broad (>120 ms) Rhythm Regular Irregular Ventricular rate (bpm) QRS width (ms) Onset Abrupt Gradual Unknown P waves Not visible / hidden P before each QRS Retrograde P after QRS Saw-tooth flutter waves ≥3 P morphologies No P waves Independent P (AV dissociation) RP interval Unknown Short (hidden/<70 ms) Long (>70 ms) Adenosine / vagal response Not given Terminates Unmasks atrial activity No effect QRS morphology Constant Monomorphic Polymorphic / twisting Delta wave / short PR in sinus rhythm Prior MI, CAD, structural disease, LV dysfunction Fusion or capture beats Concordance V1–V6 Same BBB pattern on prior sinus ECG Long QT / QT-prolonging drug COPD / lung disease Unstable: hypotension, chest pain, HF, reduced consciousness Safety alerts Check K+, Mg2+, Ca2+ and obtain a prior sinus-rhythm ECG. Refer all patients to a cardiologist/EP. 1 . AVNRT 56 % Why: Abrupt, retrograde P hidden in/after QRS, short RP, adenosine-responsive (~60% of narrow regular SVT) Action: Vagal manoeuvres (Valsalva) → IV adenosine 6-18 mg rapid + flush → verapamil/beta blocker; ablation curative (~1% AV block risk). 2 . Orthodromic AVRT (accessory pathway) 22 % Why: Retrograde P midway between QRS (long RP) and/or delta wave in sinus rhythm Action: Vagal/adenosine; flecainide/propafenone if structurally normal; DCCV if unstable; refer EP for ablation (>95% success). 3 . Atrial flutter (typical) 22 % Why: Saw-tooth flutter waves (−ve inferior, +ve V1), ventricular rate ~150 (2:1), adenosine unmasks waves Action: Rate control + anticoagulation; offer cavotricuspid isthmus ablation (~95% cure); 1:1 conduction → urgent. Decision support from rule-based scoring (not a probability). Confirm on a 12-lead ECG and clinical context. Management notes in the source deck predate current AF guidance (e.g. CHADS₂ → CHA₂DS₂-VASc). sports (rugby, martial arts, boxing) indefinitely because of the risk of a direct blow to the device or leads, unless your team specifically discusses a protective option with you. • For sports with a https://warfarin-guide.vercel.app/.text: Warfarin Guide | Anticoagulation Companion ❤️ Warfarin Guide Your Complete Anticoagulation Companion 🇬🇧 English E 🇮🇳 हिंदी ह 🇧🇩 বাংলা ব 🇮🇳 ਪੰਜਾਬੀ ਪ 💊 Overview 🩸 Dosing & Monitoring 🥦 Food & Diet ⚗️ Medicines 🛡️ Safety 🚨 Emergency Signs What is Warfarin? Warfarin is an anticoagulant ("blood thinner") that increases the time it takes your blood to clot, reducing the chance of harmful blood clots in your body. 💉 Generic: Warfarin Brand names: Coumadin®, Jantoven® Why Do You Need It? Conditions treated with warfarin: 🦵 Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT) — blood clot in a vein 🫁 Pulmonary Embolism (PE) — blood clot in the lung 🧠 Stroke / TIA — blood clot in the brain 💓 Atrial Fibrillation (AF) — irregular heartbeat ⚙️ Mechanical heart valve replacement ❤️‍🩹 Heart attack (Myocardial Infarction) How Does It Work? Warfarin works by blocking vitamin K, which is essential for clot formation. Higher vitamin K intake can reduce warfarin's effectiveness. ⚖️ Warfarin ↔ Vitamin K Balance 📉 More Vit K = Lower INR = Clot risk 📈 Less Vit K = Higher INR = Bleed risk For informational purposes only. Always follow your doctor's instructions. https://inotropes-ds.vercel.app/.text: CS Vasoactive Selector — Cardiogenic Shock Inotrope/Vasopressor Decision Support Vasoactive Selector Research Hub Data Analysis Hub EMC Digitals · Clinical Decision Support Vasoactive Selector — Cardiogenic Shock Logic derived from Riccardi et al., Eur J Heart Fail 2024;26:411–431 (Figures 2–3, Table 2). For clinician use alongside bedside judgment and haemodynamic monitoring — not a substitute for either. Vasopressor treatment stage MECHANICAL EFFICIENCY Mechanical efficiency Mechanical inefficiency Metabolic inefficiency Patient profile Select the closest match — recommendations update live. Aetiology AMI-CS Acute myocardial infarction — culprit vessel revascularised or being revascularised ADHF-CS Acute decompensated heart failure — de novo or chronic HF decompensation RV-predominant CS Right ventricular failure driving the shock state Haemodynamic profile Hypotension prevails SBP <90 mmHg or MAP <65 mmHg — perfusion pressure is the immediate threat "Normotensive" CS Low cardiac output / hypoperfusion without marked hypotension Chronic β-blocker therapy Yes Favours agents that bypass the β-adrenergic receptor No / unknown Renal function Significant impairment Milrinone is renally cleared — use with caution, adjust dose Normal / mild impairment Bradycardia risk Persistent / significant bradycardia Favours agents with chronotropic support; pacing if persistent No Recommendation AMI-CS Hypotension prevails Mechanical efficiency First-line Rescue phase If refractory / second-line Escalation Scope of evidence. Per the source review: no pharmacological therapy has proven mortality benefit in cardiogenic shock (DOREMI, LIDO, SURVIVE, SOAP-II and the Cochrane meta-analysis were consistently neutral or only hypothesis-generating). This tool encodes a therapeutic algorithm built from a mix of RCTs and observational registries where trial data is absent, and is intended to structure — not replace — bedside decision-making, invasive haemodynamic assessment, and escalation planning to MCS. Built on Riccardi M, Pagnesi M, Chioncel O, et al. Medical therapy of cardiogenic shock: contemporary use of inotropes and vasopressors. Eur J Heart Fail . 2024;26:411–431. doi:10.1002/ejhf.3162 — dosing figures drawn from the article text (norepinephrine, dobutamine, milrinone, levosimendan, epinephrine, vasopressin sections). • , renal: • , brady: • , caption: • Milrinone • Levosimendan • Dobutamine • Epinephrine + sodium nitroprusside • Norepinephrine • Vasopressin • Consider add-on in vasoplegia — limited CS-specific dosing data • 0.0625–0.5 µg/kg/min (renally cleared — caution in impairment) • Standard trial regimens ~0.1 µg/kg/min infusion (see LIDO/SURVIVE dosing) • Epinephrine per protocol + nitroprusside for afterload — reserve for select ADHF-CS, monitor lactate closely • Vasopressor of choice in CS with hypotension — safer than dopamine (SOAP-II), vasopressin, or epinephrine (OptimaCC), with lower arrhythmia risk. • Not first-line as monotherapy (OptimaCC: higher refractory shock vs norepinephrine) — only in the specific ADHF-CS pathway with afterload co-management. • Logical switch once vasoplegia/metabolic inefficiency dominates — avoids further catecholamine-driven adrenoreceptor desensitisation. • badgeAet • AMI-CS • ADHF-CS • RV-predominant CS • badgeHd • hypo • Hypotension prevails • "Normotensive" CS • firstLine • secondLine • flags • Metabolic-inefficiency stage: consider replacing norepinephrine rather than escalating its dose further. • Combine with an inodilator once hypotension is the dominant problem despite initial inotrope, or vice versa. • flag warn

indicates proximal RCA occlusion with associated Right Ventricular Infarction. • ST elevation in leads I, aVL, V5, V6 accompanied by ST depression in V1-V3 points to Left Circumflex Artery (LCx) occlusion or a dominant circumflex vessel. • ST depression in V1 and V2 in inferior MI signifies concomitant posterior wall infarction of the left ventricle. • Algorithm for Inferior MI Culprit Artery (NEJM Fig. 1) • Stepwise algorithmic triage of ST elevation patterns in leads II, III, aVF and reciprocal leads: • Right Coronary Artery (RCA) Occlusion • Sensitivity 90%, Specificity 71%, PPV 94%, NPV 70% • Above RCA criteria MET + ST elevation in V1, V4R, or both • Proximal RCA Occlusion with Right Ventricular Infarction • Above criteria NOT met, and ST elevation in I, aVL, V5, and V6 with ST depression in V1, V2, and V3 • Left Circumflex Coronary Artery (LCx) Occlusion • Sensitivity 83%, Specificity 96%, PPV 91%, NPV 93% • Proximal RCA occlusion with RV infarction predisposes to profound hypotension upon administration of nitrates or diuretics due to preload dependence. Treatment mandates aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation and avoidance of venodilators. • Confusing RV infarction current-of-injury extending to V1-V3 as an acute anterior STEMI. • Failing to recognize reciprocal ST depression in V1-V3 as true posterior transmural infarction. • anterior_mi_lad • ischemia_infarction • Anterior Myocardial Infarction: LAD Occlusion Site Localization • Determining Proximal vs. Distal LAD Occlusion Relative to First Septal and First Diagonal Branches • ST-segment elevation in leads V1, V2, and V3 indicates left anterior descending (LAD) coronary artery occlusion. The level of LAD occlusion directly predicts infarct size, cardiogenic shock risk, and conduction system necrosis. • Proximal LAD occlusion (before the 1st septal and 1st diagonal branches) directs the ST vector upward toward aVL, V1, and aVR, and away from inferior leads. • Algorithm for Anterior MI Culprit Artery (NEJM Fig. 2) • Classification of LAD occlusion site based on V1, bundle branch pattern, and inferior lead changes: • Proximal LAD Occlusion • Sensitivity 12%, Specificity 100%, PPV 100%, NPV 61% • Sensitivity 34%, Specificity 98%, PPV 93%, NPV 68% • Distal LAD Occlusion (or Wrap-Around LAD) • Sensitivity 66%, Specificity 73%, PPV 78%, NPV 62% • Proximal LAD occlusion threatens a large myocardial territory including the interventricular septum, anterior wall, and conduction system (bundle of His and bundle branches), resulting in a high risk of pump failure and sudden complete heart block. • Misdiagnosing a wrap-around LAD with simultaneous inferior and anterior ST elevation as multi-vessel disease or pericarditis. • Missing acute RBBB with QR pattern in V1 as simply a conduction defect rather than acute proximal LAD STEMI with impending pump failure. • lbbb_infarction • Acute Myocardial Infarction in the Presence of Left Bundle Branch Block • Sgarbossa Criteria, Primary vs. Secondary ST Changes, and Atypical Signs • LBBB alters both early and late phases of ventricular depolarization and produces secondary ST-T changes (discordance). Q waves cannot be used normally because early septal activation is reversed (right to left). Primary ST changes concordant with the QRS vector indicate acute myocardial infarction. • Presence of QR complexes in leads I, aVL, V5, or V6 with LBBB strongly suggests underlying infarction with septal involvement. • Notching of the ascending limb of a wide S wave in midprecordial leads (Cabrera sign) or wide R wave in V5-V6 (Chapman sign) suggests chronic myocardial infarction. • New or presumably new LBBB in a patient with acute ischemic chest pain is treated as a STEMI equivalent warranting emergent primary reperfusion therapy. • Assuming that normal discordance (ST elevation in V1-V3 with deep S wave) is always benign when ST elevation exceeds 5 mm or is concordant. • Relying on standard pathological Q waves in lateral leads (which are typically erased by altered septal activation in LBBB). • reperfusion_markers • Electrocardiographic Predictors of Reperfusion & Microvascular Reflow • ST Resolution Dynamics, Early T-Wave Inversion, and Accelerated Idioventricular Rhythm (AIVR) • Restoration of epicardial flow in the infarct-related artery does not guarantee microvascular tissue perfusion ("no-reflow" phenomenon). The 12-lead ECG is the most practical noninvasive tool to monitor real-time microvascular reperfusion. • Early T-Wave Inversion: Developing within the first 4 hours of reperfusion therapy is a highly specific marker of successful reperfusion. • Accelerated Idioventricular Rhythm (AIVR): Wide complex rhythm at 60-120 bpm initiated by a late-coupled ventricular premature beat. It is a BENIGN hallmark of reperfusion. • DO NOT SUPPRESS AIVR: Antiarrhythmics are contraindicated for AIVR because it maintains cardiac output and resolves spontaneously. • Failure of ST elevation to resolve by at least 50% within 90 minutes of fibrinolytic therapy is an urgent indication for rescue percutaneous coronary intervention. • Suppressing AIVR with lidocaine or amiodarone, which can cause severe bradycardia or asystole. • Assuming patent epicardial vessel on angiogram equates to tissue perfusion if ST segments remain markedly elevated. • conduction_pacemaker_ami • conduction_pacing • Conduction Disease & Pacemaker Indications in Acute Myocardial Infarction • Anatomy of Blood Supply, Inferior vs. Anterior Conduction Pathology, and ACC/AHA Table 1 Guidelines • The clinical behavior, pathophysiology, and management of AV block differ profoundly between inferior and anterior myocardial infarctions based on vascular anatomy. • Conduction System Blood Supply: Sinus node (60% RCA, 40% LCx), AV node (90% RCA, 10% LCx), Bundle of His (AV nodal artery of RCA + LAD septal branches), Right bundle branch & Left anterior fascicle (LAD septal perforators). • Inferior MI Conduction Blocks: Usually supranodal or nodal, mediated by vagal hyperactivity ( 24h, aminophylline-responsive). Escape rhythm is narrow (40-60 bpm), transient, resolving within 5-14 days. Pacing only if hemodynamically unstable. • Anterior MI Conduction Blocks: Result from extensive necrosis of the interventricular septum and infranodal His-Purkinje system. Escape rhythm is wide, unstable, and carries up to 80% mortality primarily due to massive pump failure. Usually preceded by new RBBB with axis shift (LAFB/LPFB). • Class I Temporary Pacing Indications: Asystole, symptomatic bradycardia/hypotension unresponsive to atropine, bilateral BBB (alternating RBBB/LBBB or alternating LAFB/LPFB), new bifascicular block with prolonged PR interval, Mobitz type II second-degree AV block. • ACC/AHA Pacemaker Indications in Acute MI (Table 1 Summary) • Class • Temporary Pacing Indications • Permanent Pacing Indications • Class I (Mandatory) • Class IIa • None • Class IIb • Persistent 2nd- or 3rd-degree AV block at the level of the AV node • Class III (Not indicated) • In anterior STEMI, the appearance of a new RBBB with left anterior fascicular block and PR prolongation carries a 30% excess risk of sudden complete heart block and mandates prophylactic temporary pacemaker placement. • Rushing to place a permanent pacemaker in acute inferior MI with transient Wenckebach or complete heart block that is hemodynamically tolerated. • Treating AIVR with antiarrhythmics or temporary pacing when it represents benign reperfusion. • biophysics_lead_systems • foundations • Biophysical Foundations, Dipoles & Lead Systems • The Cardiac Electrical Generator, Solid Angle Theorem, Einthoven Law, and Hexaxial Reference System • Mirvis & Goldberger Ch. 9 (pp. 9-1 to 9-7) • The surface ECG detects volume-conducted extracellular potential differences created by synchronized cardiac transmembrane currents. The net active wavefront at any instant is represented by a current dipole vector. • Dipole Concept: A dipole consists of a source (+ outward current) and sink (- inward current). An exploring electrode senses positive voltage when an activation wavefront moves TOWARD it, and negative voltage when moving AWAY. • Augmented Unipolar Leads: aVR, aVL, aVF use modified reference terminals excluding the exploring limb, boosting registered voltage by 50%. • Electrical Axis: Normal adult QRS axis ranges from -30° to +90°. Left axis deviation: +90°. Extreme/indeterminate: -90° to -180°. • Understanding lead geometry and vector projections allows clinicians to deduce anatomical injury zones, chamber enlargement, and fascicular blocks from frontal and precordial axes. • Misinterpreting an arm electrode cable reversal (e.g. right arm / left arm swap causes completely inverted P, QRS, and T in lead I with normal precordial progression). • Placing V1/V2 too high in the 2nd/3rd intercostal space, which creates false-positive rSr' patterns and pseudo-anterior infarction. • hypertrophy_chamber_abnormalities • hypertrophy • Atrial Abnormalities & Ventricular Hypertrophy • P Mitrale, P Pulmonale, Sokolow-Lyon, Cornell Voltage, and RVH Pressure Overload Patterns • Mirvis & Goldberger Ch. 9 (Tables 9-3, 9-4, 9-5) • Chamber enlargement produces characteristic alterations in waveform duration, amplitude, and repolarization forces due to increased myocardium mass and altered conduction pathways. • LVH Strain Pattern: Asymmetric ST depression with inverted T waves in lateral leads (I, aVL, V5, V6) indicates severe hypertrophy or subendocardial ischemia, conferring a 5-fold cardiovascular event risk. • LVH with repolarization abnormalities dramatically increases cardiovascular morbidity. Differentiating LVH strain from acute non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction is a common emergency challenge. • High false-positive rate of voltage criteria in thin, young, or athletic individuals. • electrolytes_metabolic_emergencies • electrolytes_metabolic • Electrolyte, Metabolic, Hypothermic & Drug Emergencies • Hyperkalemia T-Waves to Sine Wave, Hypokalemia U Waves, Calcium Shifts, Osborn Waves & Digitalis Toxicity • Mirvis & Goldberger Ch. 9 (pp. 9-36 to 9-40) • Systemic metabolic and electrolyte disorders profoundly alter cellular action potentials, transmembrane gradients, and conduction velocity, producing rapid life-threatening changes. • Severe Hyperkalemia Mimic: Can produce ST elevation in V1-V2 simulating an anterior current-of-injury. • Hypokalemia: Hyperpolarization and prolonged action potential cause ST depression, flattened T waves, and prominent U waves (exceeding T wave amplitude, QU prolongation), predisposing to Torsades de Pointes. • Triad of Chronic Renal Failure: Peaked T waves (hyperkalemia) + prolonged QT/ST (hypocalcemia) + LVH (hypertension). • Calcium Disturbances: Hypercalcemia abbreviates phase 2, shortening the QT interval. Hypocalcemia prolongs phase 2, lengthening the ST segment and QT interval. • Systemic Hypothermia: Produces a prominent convex deflection at the J point called the Osborn wave (J wave), accompanied by sinus bradycardia, prolonged intervals, and muscle tremor artifact. • Digitalis Effect vs. Toxicity: "Scooped" downsloping ST-T depression with short QT (therapeutic effect). Toxicity causes paroxysmal junctional tachycardia with exit block, bidirectional VT, and AV block. • Total Electrical Alternans: Beat-to-beat alternation of P-QRS-T amplitude with sinus tachycardia is highly specific for pericardial effusion with cardiac tamponade ("swinging heart"). • Rapid recognition of hyperkalemic sine waves or hypokalemic QU prolongation enables immediate administration of membrane-stabilizing IV calcium gluconate or potassium/magnesium repletion before fatal arrest. • Mistaking hyperkalemic peaked T waves for hyperacute ischemic T waves (hyperkalemic T waves are typically narrow-based, symmetrical, and tented with normal or short QT). • Suppressing ventricular escape rhythms in severe hyperkalemia or digoxin toxicity with sodium channel blockers. • stemi_mimics_pseudoinfarctions • guidelines_pitfalls • STEMI Mimics, Pseudoinfarctions & Noninfarction Q Waves • Acute Pericarditis vs. Infarct, Early Repolarization, Pulmonary Embolism S1Q3T3, and Artifacts • Mirvis & Goldberger Ch. 9 (Tables 9-9, 9-10, 9-11 & Fig. 9-48) • Numerous non-coronary conditions simulate acute myocardial infarction or ischemia on the 12-lead ECG. Precise differentiation prevents inappropriate fibrinolysis or delayed emergency interventions. • Acute Pericarditis: Characterized by diffuse, concave-upward ST-segment elevation across almost all leads (I, II, aVF, V2-V6). Hallmark PR-segment depression in inferolateral leads with reciprocal PR elevation in aVR (atrial injury current). Absence of reciprocal ST depression (except aVR/V1) and absence of pathological Q waves. • Benign Early Repolarization: Concave ST elevation most prominent in V4-V5 with notched or slurred J-point ("fish-hook" pattern), tall upright symmetrical T waves, and absence of reciprocal ST depression. • Pulmonary Embolism (Acute Cor Pulmonale): S1Q3T3 pattern (S in lead I, Q and T-wave inversion in lead III), T-wave inversions in right precordial leads V1-V4, QR in V1, new incomplete or complete RBBB, and sinus tachycardia. • Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HCM): Dagger-like, deep, narrow noninfarction Q waves in inferolateral leads (II, III, aVF, V4-V6) caused by massive septal hypertrophy. • Administering thrombolytic therapy to an acute pericarditis or aortic dissection patient misdiagnosed as STEMI can cause catastrophic hemorrhagic tamponade or exsanguination. • Diagnosing STEMI without looking for reciprocal ST depression in opposing leads. • Failing to inspect lead aVR for PR elevation in suspected pericarditis. • bg-emerald-600 text-white shadow-sm • bg-slate-800 text-slate-400 hover:text-slate-200 • ,o.length, • bg-slate-800 border-emerald-500 shadow-md ring-1 ring-emerald-500/40 text-white • bg-slate-900/80 border-slate-800 hover:bg-slate-800/60 text-slate-300 • fill-amber-400 text-amber-400 • Bookmark • ,caseRefId: • ,vignette: • ,leadPreview: • ,question: • ,text: • ,isCorrect:!1,explanation: • ,isCorrect:!0,explanation: • ,sourceReference: • myocardial blush • ,children:[o, • ,children:[e+1, • ,Math.round(o/Ae.length*100), • ,m.lead, • :t&&!e.isCorrect? ECG Learning Atlas — 33 lessons & source tracings 1. Upload ECG Accepted formats: PDF, JPG, JPEG, PNG 2. Patient Information Age Sex Male Female Other Clinical Background 3. Analysis Mode Automated Parsing Gemini reads the ECG and derives rate, axis, and intervals itself. Manual Input Work through the checklist yourself; AI cross-checks your findings. Chapter knowledge base Braunwald, Chapter 9: Electrocardiography — David M. Mirvis and Ary L. Goldberger; supplied PDF, headers dated March 2004. Page numbers refer to PDF pages. Foundational ECG interpretation; current management requires current guidelines. Calibration and systematic interpretation · PDF pp. 7–12, 38–39 Check lead placement, signal quality, paper speed and voltage calibration before measuring intervals. At 25 mm/s a small square represents 40 ms. Interpret rate, rhythm, P waves, PR, QRS, axis and ST-T/QT together. QRS and conduction · PDF pp. 11, 18–23 A QRS duration of 120 ms or more warrants assessment for conduction delay. Duration alone cannot identify right or left bundle branch block: lead-specific morphology is needed. Short PR with a delta wave and altered QRS suggests preexcitation. Ventricular repolarization and QT · PDF pp. 12, 34–36 Bazett correction divides QT by the square root of RR in seconds. QT varies with heart rate and sex; verify the end of the T wave and exclude U waves. Drug and electrolyte effects can alter repolarization. A single corrected value does not establish a long-QT syndrome. Electrical axis · PDF pp. 7–8, 20 Limb-lead polarity estimates the QRS quadrant. Positive lead I with negative aVF requires lead II to distinguish a leftward normal axis from left axis deviation. Fascicular block requires characteristic morphology and exclusion of alternative causes. Ischemia and ST-T changes · PDF pp. 24–32 ST elevation, ST depression and T-wave changes require interpretation with distribution, morphology, symptoms and prior tracings. Ischemia may occur without diagnostic ST-T changes. Nonischemic causes include early repolarization, pericarditis, hypertrophy and conduction abnormalities; a checkbox cannot diagnose infarction. Electrolyte effects · PDF pp. 36–37 Hyperkalemia can produce peaked T waves, PR prolongation, reduced P waves and QRS widening. Even severe hyperkalemia may lack typical ECG changes. Hypokalemia can produce prominent U waves and altered repolarization. Confirm with laboratory testing. Interpretation limits · PDF pp. 38–39 ECG findings require clinical correlation and comparison with prior records. Computer interpretation needs clinician review. Neither a normal-looking ECG nor isolated measurements exclude important cardiac disease. 4. AI Analysis Gemini will read the ECG directly and produce a full systematic interpretation. Upload an ECG to enable analysis Analyze with knowledge base (no AI) AI errors automatically use the knowledge base. Local analysis requires manual measurements and does not read images. This supports abnormal recovery but does not establish a pacing indication. • Not above the commonly used 550-ms threshold. A normal value does not exclude clinical SND. • Temporary pacing • Bridge to recovery or definitive therapy • Reassess the underlying cause, capture, sensing and ongoing need daily. A pacing spike or broad complex alone does not prove mechanical capture. • ALS25 • Dual-chamber DDD(R) • Preserve AV synchrony in sinus rhythm • Requires an atrial lead and suitable atrial sensing/capture. Atrial tracking during tachyarrhythmia needs mode switching. Unnecessary RV pacing and excessively long AV delays can both be harmful. • Check wound, lead integrity, thresholds, sensing, AV timing, mode-switch episodes, AF burden and ventricular pacing percentage. In SND minimize unnecessary ventricular pacing safely. • Match the mode to the physiology • VVI in sinus rhythm may cause loss of AV synchrony and pacemaker syndrome. VDD requires dependable sinus activity and atrial sensing. Atrial-only pacing is unsuitable when important AV disease exists. • Reassess atrial rhythm, AV conduction, symptoms and sensor response. The five-letter pacing code describes chamber paced, chamber sensed, response, rate modulation and multisite functions. • Avoid a conventional pocket and transvenous lead • Consider when an appropriate pacing indication exists and lead/pocket infection risk, venous access or anatomy favors it. Single-chamber, atrial-mechanical tracking and dual-chamber leadless technologies have distinct capabilities. • Discuss vascular injury, perforation, retrieval, battery depletion, future device accumulation and upgrade strategy. Leadless does not mean complication-free and does not itself expand pacing indications. • Resynchronize a dyssynchronous ventricle • Verify effective BiV capture and high delivery percentage, lead thresholds, phrenic stimulation, symptoms and remodeling. BioPace did not prove routine BiV superiority in its predominantly preserved-EF population. • His-bundle pacing • Recruit the proximal native conduction system • Potential constraints include higher/rising thresholds, sensing problems, lead revision, battery use and failure to correct distal disease. Pacemaker-dependent patients may need a backup ventricular lead. • Document 12-lead output transitions, His and myocardial thresholds, BBB-correction threshold where relevant, sensing and programmed safety margin. A narrow paced QRS alone is not complete proof of His capture. • Left bundle branch area pacing • A distal route to physiological activation • LBBAP places a lead deep in the interventricular septum to recruit left-sided conduction. It may provide a useful alternative to HBP or conventional RV pacing in selected patients. Distinguish true left bundle/fascicular capture from LV septal myocardial pacing. • Assess conduction-capture criteria rather than relying only on an RBBB-like V1 pattern or one activation-time cutoff. Risks include septal perforation, coronary injury, lead instability and uncertain aspects of long-term extraction. • Record capture transitions, thresholds, sensing, impedance, V6 activation timing and serial ECGs. The supplied chapter’s absolute statements about uniformly low thresholds or purely observational evidence should not be treated as timeless facts. • Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator • Prevent death from ventricular tachyarrhythmia • A pacemaker indication does not automatically imply an ICD. Conversely, sarcoidosis or some genetic cardiomyopathies may require defibrillator assessment despite preserved or mildly reduced EF. A subcutaneous ICD does not supply chronic brady pacing or ATP. • Discuss shocks, ATP, inappropriate therapies, remote monitoring, lead complications, generator replacement and future shock deactivation in relation to goals of care. Device selection must include current and likely pacing needs. • Implantable loop recorder • Selected patients with infrequent unexplained syncope or suspected intermittent arrhythmia can benefit from prolonged rhythm monitoring when shorter recordings are nondiagnostic. • An ILR is not a pacemaker or defibrillator. It does not protect a patient from known high-risk advanced block. Do not postpone indicated treatment merely to obtain another recording. • An indication first.
